June 15, 2026 
 
Dr. Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services 
US Department of Health and Human Services 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244-1850 
 
Dear Administrator Oz: 
 
The Health IT End-Users Alliance (the Alliance) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Centers for 
Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Proposed Rule published in the April 14, 2026, Federal Register (CMS-0062-P). 
 
The Alliance brings together health information professionals, physicians, hospitals, and other front-line 
healthcare providers and organizations that use health information technology (IT) to ensure that policy 
and standards development activities reflect the complex web of clinical and operational challenges facing 
those who use such technologies today. By working collaboratively, the Alliance is focused on priorities for 
how technology can best support clinical care and operations.  
 
The Alliance supports CMS’ goal to improve the prior authorization process and reduce burden on end-
users. We supported and provided feedback on the policies within the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior 
Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F), and applaud CMS applying these policies to include drugs, which 
have long been a major point of frustration and burden in prior authorization for healthcare organizations 
and end-users. We support the proposals related to process improvements, including metrics reporting, 
quicker decision timeframes, and transparency on prior authorization information and application 
programming interface (API) usage, and encourage CMS to align these across all CMS-regulated and 
impacted payers. 
 
However, we caution that achieving this goal depends on successful implementation of standards, which 
will require federal support for more robust real-world testing of the interoperability standards and 
implementation guides (IGs) intended to facilitate automation. IGs guide the execution and use of a 
particular standard in care settings by defining data elements, workflows, business rules, and system 
behaviors. It is important for standards and IGs to be thoroughly tested and vetted prior to implementation 
in clinical and operational settings to avoid risk and additional burden. 
 
Executing real-world testing and achieving the goal of improved and streamlined prior authorization will 
require greater engagement with the health IT end-user and provider community to understand the effort 
required to operationalize the technology solutions and business processes needed to interact with payer 
systems. In addition to testing, the Alliance urges CMS to support end-user implementation by providing 
resources, technical assistance, and flexibilities, especially for under-resourced organizations, as they 
work to implement policies in CMS-0057-F and any forthcoming finalized policies that result from this 
proposed rule. This will ensure that the standards and IGs function as intended to support end-users truly 
conducting streamlined, electronic prior authorization. 
 
 
The Alliance supports the healthcare industry’s move from X12 standards to HL7® Fast Healthcare 
Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standards, including the proposed adoption of FHIR standards as the 
HIPAA standard for electronic prior authorization, either replacing existing X12 standards or providing a 
FHIR standard where there currently is no standard. The healthcare industry has long awaited a solution for 
the lack of an attachment standard to accompany the X12 278 transaction standard, and we appreciate 
CMS clarifying and proposing to adopt the suite of FHIR standards to support electronic prior authorization 
transactions.  
 
However, the Alliance has concerns about requiring adoption of FHIR standards and IGs that are not yet 
sufficiently mature, particularly in the absence of a clear roadmap for real-world testing and reporting that 
would demonstrate when these standards and IGs will be mature and how they can and will be 
incorporated into end-user workflows with minimal burden. This should happen before compliance is 
enforced. We encourage CMS to extend the compliance deadlines for use of the FHIR standards and 
implement flexibilities to ensure the X12 278 standard continues to be available as a method for data 
exchange as we transition to FHIR standards and IGs maturation and use in real-world settings. This would 
ensure that method of data exchange is still available until the FHIR-supported ecosystem has proven to 
work as intended. 
 
Real-world testing is a critical component of ensuring standards and IGs function as intended in real-world 
settings, support the needs of end-users, and can support the successful implementation of policies that 
rely on the use of those standards. The lack of robust real-world testing may cause increased burden on the 
end-user due to technology that is poorly designed or does not meet real-world workflows. Other 
consequences due to lack of adequate real-world testing include: 
 
• 
adoption and implementation of standards that require significant workarounds by healthcare 
organizations; 
• 
adoption and implementation of incomplete or immature standards; 
• 
standards and policies that do not achieve the desired goal when deployed; 
• 
excessive burden added to end-users; 
• 
wasted money on failed implementations; and 
• 
confusion from patients with respect to technological capabilities. 
 
By working together with end-users earlier through real-world testing, developers, impacted payers, 
healthcare organizations, and policymakers can ensure the successful streamlining and efficiency of 
electronic prior authorization with fewer burdens. As part of the Appendix to this letter, we have included 
our Real-world Testing Consensus Statement that includes further policy recommendations. 
 
Work with end-users should also extend to CMS’ continued exploratory activities related to the proposed 
rule’s request for information (RFI) on event notifications and proposals related to API endpoints. While two 
different technologies, both will require extensive input from the technology development community and 
the end-user community to ensure CMS’ policy goals are ultimately accomplished. CMS should engage in 
extensive public convenings and stakeholder requests for input processes. This will help CMS ensure any 
new policy proposals create guardrails to maintain accuracy in API endpoints, without disrupting existing 
end-user processes related to event notifications in value-based care, with the ultimate goal of improving 
the interoperable flow of data while minimizing disruption to the healthcare community. 
 
 
The proposed 24-month implementation timeline will be challenging for end-users to adhere to. With final 
rule publication, electronic health record (EHR) vendors must interpret the IG specification, build or update 
software, and release it to customers, which can take at least 12 months. Following, healthcare 
organizations need to configure, test, and validate the new functionality in their environments, as well as 
train staff, redesign workflows, and coordinate with payer partners. Ideally, after the standards and IGs are 
live, organizations will be required to monitor performance, troubleshoot issues, and retrain and redesign 
workflows where needed. Thus, we encourage CMS to consider a phased compliance timeline or finalize a 
longer implementation timeline, as well as provide support for real-world testing, technical assistance, and 
implementation of standards and IGs before enforcement. 
 
The Health IT End-Users Alliance thanks CMS for its commitment to improving electronic prior 
authorization processes, and we are committed to being a partner in this effort by providing the end-user 
perspective to strengthen these policies. To discuss our feedback further or if you have any questions, 
please contact Tara O’Donnell, Manager, Regulatory Affairs at the American Health Information 
Management Association (AHIMA) at Tara.ODonnell@ahima.org.
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Health IT End-Users Alliance
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Coalition of health information professionals, physicians, hospitals, and front-line healthcare providers/organizations that use health IT; contact via AHIMA (American Health Information Management Association)

---

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The Health IT End-Users Alliance supports CMS' goals to improve prior authorization and reduce burden on end-users, including the extension to drugs and the proposed transition from X12 to FHIR standards as the HIPAA standard for PA. However, the Alliance raises significant concerns about mandating FHIR standards and IGs that are not yet sufficiently mature, the lack of a real-world testing roadmap, and the 24-month implementation timeline being too tight. They urge phased compliance deadlines, continuation of X12 as a fallback during transition, federal technical assistance, and meaningful end-user engagement before enforcement.

---

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS, FHIR-IG-REQUIRED, IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE (cross-cutting), API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING, API-USAGE-METRICS, PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P (proposed rule); CMS-0057-F (2024 final rule)
- **Standards referenced:** HL7 FHIR, X12 278 transaction standard, FHIR implementation guides (IGs), Da Vinci IGs (implied), EHR systems

---

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Support for PA Extension to Drugs and Process Improvements**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Drugs have long been a major source of PA frustration and burden; extending electronic PA requirements is welcomed.
- **Specific request:** Align metrics reporting, timeframes, and transparency requirements across all CMS-regulated and impacted payers.

**Topic 2: Support for FHIR as HIPAA Standard for PA (with conditions)**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** The healthcare industry has long needed a solution for the lack of an attachment standard for the X12 278; FHIR fills this gap. However, compliance should not be enforced until IGs are demonstrably mature.
- **Specific request:** Extend compliance deadlines; maintain X12 278 availability as fallback during transition; require a clear roadmap for IG maturation and real-world testing before enforcement.

**Topic 3: FHIR IG Maturity and Real-World Testing**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify / Clarify
- **Rationale:** IGs are not yet sufficiently mature. Without robust real-world testing, mandating them risks workarounds, failed implementations, excessive burden, wasted resources, and patient confusion.
- **Specific request:** CMS must establish a clear real-world testing roadmap and reporting mechanism to demonstrate IG maturity before compliance is enforced. Federal support for testing is needed.

**Topic 4: Implementation Timeline**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED, HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS (cross-cutting)
- **Position:** Oppose / Modify
- **Rationale:** The 24-month timeline is insufficient: EHR vendors need ~12 months to build and release updates after final rule publication, leaving insufficient time for healthcare organizations to configure, train, test, and coordinate with payers.
- **Specific request:** Phased compliance timeline or extended implementation period, with technical assistance and real-world testing support before enforcement.

**Topic 5: API Endpoints and Event Notifications**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Both API endpoint reporting and event notifications will require extensive input from the technology development and end-user communities.
- **Specific request:** CMS should conduct extensive public convenings and stakeholder input processes to develop guardrails that ensure API endpoint accuracy without disrupting existing value-based care event notification workflows.

---

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1/S37:** Commenter raises concerns about requiring IGs before they are mature enough; calls for real-world testing evidence before mandating adoption. Existing experience with standards that were adopted before sufficient testing shows risk of burdensome workarounds.
- **S44:** Supports FHIR as the appropriate standard for PA transactions; welcomes resolution of the long-standing gap in the X12 278 attachment standard.
- **S46:** Supports FHIR replacing X12 but requests X12 278 remain available as a fallback until FHIR ecosystem proves out in real-world settings.
- **S47:** The 24-month compliance timeline is too short given EHR vendor build time (~12 months) plus organizational configuration, training, and testing requirements. Urges phased or extended timeline.
- **S50:** FHIR IGs are not yet sufficiently mature; a clear roadmap for real-world testing and maturation reporting is needed before compliance is enforced.
- **S53:** Supports phased compliance approach rather than a single hard deadline.
- **S23/S24:** Supports stakeholder engagement and public convenings around API endpoint reporting; emphasizes need to avoid disruption to existing value-based care event notification workflows.

---

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Extend compliance deadlines for FHIR standards and IGs until real-world testing demonstrates sufficient maturity.
2. Maintain X12 278 as a fallback data exchange method during the FHIR transition period.
3. Establish a clear real-world testing roadmap and reporting mechanism to demonstrate when FHIR IGs are ready for enforcement.
4. Implement a phased compliance timeline (or finalize a longer timeline) for the 24-month requirement.
5. Provide federal resources, technical assistance, and flexibilities—especially for under-resourced organizations—to support implementation.
6. Engage end-users, developers, and payers in extensive public convenings around API endpoint reporting and event notification proposals before finalizing policy.
7. Align metrics reporting, decision timeframes, and transparency requirements across all CMS-regulated and impacted payers.

---

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** FHIR IGs mandated before demonstrating real-world maturity; insufficient implementation timeline; lack of federal support for testing and end-user adoption.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Workarounds by healthcare organizations, wasted money on failed implementations, standards that don't achieve policy goals when deployed, excessive end-user burden, patient confusion.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** EHR vendor build/release cycle (~12 months), organizational configuration and training, workflow redesign, payer coordination—all compressing into the 24-month window.

---

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** EHR vendor software build and release can take at least 12 months after final rule publication.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Alliance's Real-world Testing Consensus Statement (referenced as Appendix to the letter, though not reproduced in the extracted text).
- **Examples provided:** X12 278 attachment standard gap as historical precedent for why FHIR fills a real need; description of healthcare organization implementation sequence (configure, test, validate, train, coordinate, monitor).

---

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Health IT end-users (health information professionals, physicians, hospitals, front-line providers), EHR vendors, impacted payers, under-resourced healthcare organizations.
- **Economic implications:** Risk of wasted money on failed implementations if IGs are immature; costs to EHR vendors and providers to implement within a compressed timeline.
- **Technical feasibility:** Raises material concerns—IGs are not yet sufficiently mature; 24-month timeline is inadequate given the multi-step implementation sequence required.
- **Patient care impact:** Potential patient confusion from immature technology; if done well, electronic PA for drugs will reduce burden and delays in medication access.

---

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed (supportive of goals, concerned about execution)
- **Tone:** Collaborative, Professional
- **Priority level:** High

---

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "However, the Alliance has concerns about requiring adoption of FHIR standards and IGs that are not yet sufficiently mature, particularly in the absence of a clear roadmap for real-world testing and reporting that would demonstrate when these standards and IGs will be mature and how they can and will be incorporated into end-user workflows with minimal burden." - Context: Core objection to the pace of IG mandates under FHIR-IG-REQUIRED and HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS.

2. "We encourage CMS to extend the compliance deadlines for use of the FHIR standards and implement flexibilities to ensure the X12 278 standard continues to be available as a method for data exchange as we transition to FHIR standards and IGs maturation and use in real-world settings." - Context: Specific policy request to avoid abandoning X12 prematurely.

3. "The proposed 24-month implementation timeline will be challenging for end-users to adhere to. With final rule publication, electronic health record (EHR) vendors must interpret the IG specification, build or update software, and release it to customers, which can take at least 12 months." - Context: Explanation of why 24 months is insufficient for the full implementation chain.

4. "The lack of robust real-world testing may cause increased burden on the end-user due to technology that is poorly designed or does not meet real-world workflows." - Context: Central argument for why real-world testing must precede enforcement.

---

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - 24-month timeline is insufficient given EHR vendor build cycles and organizational implementation steps; urges phased or extended deadlines.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Warns of wasted money on failed implementations; calls for federal technical assistance especially for under-resourced organizations.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Core concern: immature IGs and rushed timelines add burden rather than reduce it; end-user burden is the organizing concern throughout.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Questions whether the 24-month timeline is achievable and whether IGs are mature enough for real-world deployment.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Central theme: FHIR IGs not yet sufficiently mature; real-world testing roadmap required before enforcement.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Calls for extensive public convenings and end-user engagement on API endpoints, event notifications, and IG testing.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Concerns about disruption to existing value-based care event notification workflows; X12 278 should remain available during transition.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - EHR vendor build/release timelines (~12 months) are a key constraint; vendor readiness is central to the timeline argument.
